extracted.intended_audience: graduate students and instructors learning or teaching the foundations of algebraic geometry
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and conventions for using and teaching a rigorous, first-year-style foundations textbook on algebraic geometry (schemes, sheaves, cohomology). Covers pedagogical choices, prerequisites, scope, and notation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Importance of exercises
rubrics_metrics.description: This book has a lot of exercises; they are interspersed throughout the exposition (not left to the end). Some exercises are trivial, some necessary ones may be hard, and most have been field-tested.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Readers should work through a significant number of exercises to fix ideas; learning is primarily by doing, not by passive reading. Hints may help but sometimes will not; failure to do exercises is strongly discouraged (authorial admonition).

rubrics_metrics.name: Numbering and presentation conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Everything is numbered by chapter and section consistently for ease of reference; exercises are indicated by letters and sprinkled throughout; individual paragraphs often get numbers; definitions are in bold and sometimes given in passing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the numbering for precise reference; expect a tightly structured layout that facilitates cross-referencing in courses and seminars.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain geometric motivation
rubrics_metrics.description: When introduced to a new idea, always ask why you should care and try to apply any new abstraction to some concrete example you can understand well.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not be seduced by untethered abstraction; hold tight to geometric intuition while learning formal structures. Expect the text to encourage concrete examples alongside abstract theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Early introduction of schemes (but keep affine varieties central)
rubrics_metrics.description: The author encourages learning about schemes immediately while treating affine complex varieties as the central (but not exclusive) motivating example.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Build intuition for schemes from affine complex varieties; be aware of the three simultaneous generalizations (nilpotents, gluing, and working over general rings) and use them to ground understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pedagogical choice: prefer direct/naive exposition when helpful
rubrics_metrics.description: If two approaches exist and one is more direct and natural from a naive point of view, the book prefers that approach over the more 'correct' advanced viewpoint.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instructors may reverse these choices; the book's exposition is intentionally learner-centered even at the cost of postponing maximal generality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cohomology pedagogy: Čech before derived functors
rubrics_metrics.description: Cohomology is developed first using Čech cohomology (as Serre did), with derived functor cohomology introduced later.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although Grothendieck considered this accidental, the author argues Čech-first is the right way for most learners; derived functors are presented after the homological algebra background is understood.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimize unnecessary hypotheses
rubrics_metrics.description: State results with as few hypotheses as the proof justifies; avoid adding hypotheses that are not needed for the proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Noetherian hypotheses are included only when necessary; include helpful hypotheses when they make proofs cleaner and more memorable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish coherent vs finite-type quasicoherent sheaves
rubrics_metrics.description: Even in the Noetherian situation where coherent = finite type, the book distinguishes these notions in statements and exercises to make clear what is used in proofs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This distinction helps readers remember exactly when Noetherian hypotheses matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quasiseparatedness emphasized early
rubrics_metrics.description: Quasiseparatedness is introduced early and used often instead of routinely assuming Noetherian hypotheses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The trade-off is remembering one extra word, but once learned, quasiseparatedness clarifies why and when certain results hold; many schemes of interest are quasiseparated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of starred sections
rubrics_metrics.description: Sections marked with ⋆ are optional material worth knowing on a later reading; sections marked with ⋆⋆ are not intended for first reading and should be skipped unless the reader really wants them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow the star-marking as a guide to which material is essential vs optional for a first course or first pass.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intended scope and learning goals
rubrics_metrics.description: The book aims to give a serious, reasonably complete introduction to foundations of algebraic geometry that is digestible over a single year; after a year readers should have a broad familiarity, be ready for seminars, know examples, and be able to work through details.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The book is challenging but designed as a first introduction with enough examples and calculations; it is not encyclopedic and generally omits analytic aspects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prerequisite background
rubrics_metrics.description: Readers should be familiar with basic commutative ring theory (ideals, prime/maximal ideals, localization), module theory (tensor products, exact sequences), some field theory, and some topology; manifolds are used for motivation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: References: recommend texts in commutative algebra ([E], [AtM], [Mat2]), homological algebra ([Weib]), and the Stacks Project for reference material; having other books on hand is helpful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conventions on rings and set theory
rubrics_metrics.description: All rings are assumed commutative (unless stated), contain a unit (1), the 0-ring is allowed, and the book accepts the Axiom of Choice (used e.g., to assert existence of maximal ideals and enough injectives). Notation: (A, m) or (A, m, k) for local rings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These foundational conventions should be assumed throughout; readers with concerns about set-theoretic issues are pointed to references but are told the book will not dwell on them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instructor guidance for course planning
rubrics_metrics.description: If used for a course, adapt the book to your own point of view and goals; pick an application/theorem to reach, pace the course accordingly, and use Figure 0.1 (chapter dependency graph) to map out prerequisites.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author suggests ending with curves (Chapter 19) or the 27 lines (Chapter 27) as good capstones; do not feel compelled to sprint to the end—ending at the right place is better.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emphasize examples and pathologies
rubrics_metrics.description: Pathological and counterexamples are pedagogical tools ('warning sticks') that indicate where hypotheses matter; they provide reality checks when evaluating statements or conjectures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Learn recurring counterexamples and pathologies (e.g., two planes meeting at a point) to understand limits of theorems; use examples to consolidate understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of generality in proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Results are generally stated in the maximal generality that the proof justifies, but the book will not give a much harder proof solely to obtain greater generality unless it is useful for later material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Readers are invited to ignore greater generality when it is not needed; some theorems are proved in extra generality (e.g., proper morphisms rather than projective) when pedagogically valuable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advice about learning sequence and stepping stones
rubrics_metrics.description: Pay attention to crucial stepping stones (e.g., category theory, sheaf theory) as these small parts build the subject; chapters 1–2 prepare the reader for the rest by teaching language and tools.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Invest time early in foundational chapters even if they feel slow—they payoff later by enabling cleaner thinking and using tools effectively.
